action_criteria.expected_evidence: AChR binding antibody 0.9 nmol/L (reference <0.5) with raised blocking and modulating antibodies; TSH normal; HbA1c 7.8%.
action_criteria.label: Order AChR binding antibody and thyroid function
action_criteria.rationale: Fatigable ptosis, diplopia, fatigable chewing and nasal speech with proximal weakness point to generalized MG; AChR binding antibody is the first test and thyroid function is tested in every MG patient (Jacob 2025, Evoli 2019).

action_criteria.rationale: Neurophysiology confirms the junctional disorder and, with normal CMAPs and no facilitation, argues against LEMS, which his smoking history and cancer history raise (Jacob 2025).

prohibited_recommendations: Avoid fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides, macrolides and IV magnesium unless no alternative exists and the patient is monitored; use non-depolarising neuromuscular blockers only at reduced dose with quantitative monitoring.

Do not start high-dose prednisone (above 20 mg/day) as an outpatient; start low and titrate, or start high dose only with inpatient monitoring, because initial steroid-induced worsening can precipitate crisis.
Do not prescribe a penicillin (documented hives).
required_recommendations: Start pyridostigmine 30 mg orally three to four times daily and titrate to effect, monitoring bronchial secretions and wheeze because of his COPD; continue tiotropium.

Refer to thoracic surgery for resection of the anterior mediastinal nodule (presumed thymoma) once MG is controlled, with pre-operative pulmonary assessment for his COPD and pre-operative IVIG (2 g/kg) or plasma exchange because of bulbar and respiratory muscle weakness (Sanders 2016).

Start prednisone low (10-20 mg/day, increased by 5-10 mg every 3-7 days) or at high dose only with inpatient monitoring, with capillary glucose monitoring and insulin added or adjusted by the diabetes team, since prednisone will raise glucose beyond what metformin controls (HbA1c 7.8%).
Plan a steroid-sparing agent (azathioprine after TPMT/NUDT15 testing) if long-term immunosuppression is needed.

For a COPD exacerbation needing antibiotics, avoid fluoroquinolones, macrolides and aminoglycosides; doxycycline is a reasonable choice, and his penicillin allergy (hives) excludes amoxicillin and other penicillins.

Repeat MIP, MEP and FVC to follow the trend, with ICU-level care if FVC falls below 20 mL/kg, MIP is weaker than -30 cmH2O, MEP falls below 40 cmH2O, or bulbar weakness compromises cough or secretions.

avoided_actions.rationale: MG is a disorder of the neuromuscular junction; EEG has no diagnostic role here (Jacob 2025).
CSF has no role in MG; he has no ataxia, areflexia or CNS sign to raise a CSF-informative alternative (Jacob 2025).
FDG-PET is not indicated in MG; contrast CT characterizes the mediastinal nodule and shows no lung lesion (Jacob 2025).
A brain MRI was already reported normal; with positive AChR antibodies and RNS and no central signs a repeat adds nothing (Jacob 2025).

accepted: Myasthenia gravis, generalized (MGFA Class IIb), AChR antibody-positive, with thymoma; complicated by COPD, type 2 diabetes, and low-risk prostate cancer

differential.key_features: Smoking history raises the question of SCLC-associated LEMS; against it: normal baseline CMAPs, 5% post-exercise increment (no facilitation), preserved reflexes, no autonomic symptoms, no lung lesion on CT, and positive AChR antibodies.
COPD can cause dyspnea but does not produce fatigable ptosis, diplopia, or RNS decrement.
Cervical spine disease can cause weakness but not fatigable ptosis/diplopia or NMJ-pattern RNS.
Diabetic microvascular cranial neuropathy is monocular and acute, not bilateral and fluctuating.
No fixed lateralized deficit or long-tract signs; the brain MRI done by his primary care physician was reportedly normal; the deficits fluctuate.

key_clinical_evidence: Fatigable asymmetric ptosis, diplopia, fatigable chewing, nasal speech and proximal weakness worse in the afternoon: generalized MG with bulbar involvement (MGFA IIb).
AChR binding antibody 0.9 nmol/L with raised blocking and modulating antibodies, and a postsynaptic RNS decrement (masseter 14%, nasalis 11%) with normal CMAPs and no facilitation.

Mediastinal CT with contrast is indicated in every patient with MG to detect thymoma. Here it shows a 2.2 cm encapsulated anterior mediastinal nodule most consistent with thymoma, an indication for resection.
COPD (FEV1/FVC 0.58) and respiratory muscle weakness (MIP -40, MEP 62 cmH2O) coexist; surgery and steroid plans must account for both.
Type 2 diabetes with HbA1c 7.8%: corticosteroids need a glucose plan; penicillin allergy and MG-unsafe antibiotics narrow the choice for COPD exacerbations.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Emphysema is chronic and expected after 40 pack-years; it does not explain fatigable ptosis, diplopia or chewing fatigue. The actionable finding is the anterior mediastinal nodule.
red_herrings.data_point: Bilateral upper-lobe emphysematous changes (chronic COPD) on CT
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute dyspnea solely to COPD and miss MG/thymoma diagnosis.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Diabetic cranial mononeuropathy is acute, often painful and affects a single nerve without fatigability; this is bilateral, fluctuating and fatigable with bulbar and limb involvement.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor on diabetes-related cranial neuropathy as the cause of ptosis/diplopia.

sequence_constraints.reason: AChR antibody testing precedes single-fiber EMG; SFEMG is reserved for seronegative patients or a normal RNS (Jacob 2025).
Repetitive nerve stimulation is done first; SFEMG follows when RNS is normal (Jacob 2025).

findings.description: Well-circumscribed, encapsulated soft tissue nodule in the thymic bed. No calcification. Preserved fat planes with the pericardium, great vessels and pleura.
Centrilobular emphysematous changes in both upper lobes. No pulmonary nodule or mass.
No mediastinal or hilar lymphadenopathy. No pleural or pericardial effusion.

body_imaging.impression: 1. Well-circumscribed 2.2 x 1.8 x 2.0 cm homogeneously enhancing anterior mediastinal nodule without features of invasion; appearance most consistent with a thymoma. 2. Bilateral upper-lobe centrilobular emphysema. No pulmonary nodule or lymphadenopathy.

contraindications: Pyridostigmine: mechanical intestinal or urinary obstruction.
interactions: Pyridostigmine + tiotropium: no interaction at the neuromuscular junction. Tiotropium is an inhaled muscarinic (M3) antagonist without nicotinic action; it does not reduce the effect of pyridostigmine on muscle strength and may blunt its airway muscarinic effects. Continue both.
Pyridostigmine + albuterol, losartan, tamsulosin: no clinically relevant interaction.
Pyridostigmine + metformin: no pharmacokinetic interaction; gastrointestinal adverse effects (diarrhea, cramps) may be additive.
pyridostigmine.summary: No interaction requiring a change to the current medicines; caution with bronchial secretions in COPD.
warnings: Pyridostigmine increases bronchial secretions and can provoke bronchospasm: use with caution in COPD and asthma and monitor sputum and wheeze.

Benign prostatic hyperplasia on tamsulosin: pyridostigmine is contraindicated in mechanical urinary obstruction and can increase urinary urgency; confirm there is no urinary retention before starting.
Drugs that impair neuromuscular transmission (aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, macrolides, IV magnesium, neuromuscular blockers, beta-blockers) can worsen myasthenic weakness.

labs.interpretation: Anti-AChR binding antibody positive (0.9 nmol/L), with raised blocking (25%) and modulating (35%) antibodies. Anti-MuSK negative. Glucose 142 mg/dL and HbA1c 7.8% raised. Blood count, sodium, creatinine, TSH and free T4 within reference ranges. Anti-AChR antibodies are found in most patients with generalized myasthenia gravis; clinical correlation recommended.

myasthenia gravis diagnosis thymoma thym.query: myasthenia gravis diagnosis thymoma thymectomy guidance

results.finding: Pyridostigmine is the initial symptomatic treatment; corticosteroids or immunosuppressive therapy are used when treatment goals are not met; thymectomy is recommended for thymoma and should be considered in AChR-positive generalized MG; IVIG and plasma exchange are used for impending or manifest crisis and before surgery in patients with significant bulbar or respiratory weakness.
results.source: Sanders DB et al., Neurology 2016;87:419-425 (international consensus guidance)

results.finding: Thymectomy recommendations were updated after MGTX for non-thymomatous AChR-positive generalized MG aged 18-65; eculizumab is an option in severe refractory AChR-positive generalized MG; methotrexate may be considered as a steroid-sparing agent.
results.source: Narayanaswami P et al., Neurology 2021;96:114-122 (2020 update)

results.finding: Extended transsternal thymectomy plus prednisone improved the time-weighted quantitative MG score and reduced prednisone requirement over three years compared with prednisone alone in non-thymomatous AChR-positive generalized MG.
results.source: Wolfe GI et al., N Engl J Med 2016;375:511-522 (MGTX)

myasthenia gravis diagnosis thymoma thym.summary: Consensus guidance (Sanders DB et al., Neurology 2016;87:419-425; update Narayanaswami P et al., Neurology 2021;96:114-122) recommends AChR antibody testing first, MuSK testing when AChR antibodies are absent, and electrodiagnostic confirmation by repetitive nerve stimulation or single-fibre EMG. Chest CT or MRI is recommended in all patients to detect thymoma. In the MGTX trial (Wolfe GI et al., N Engl J Med 2016;375:511-522) thymectomy improved outcomes over three years in non-thymomatous AChR-positive generalized MG aged 18-65.

patient.chief_complaint: Drooping eyelids, double vision, and difficulty chewing

social_history.tobacco: Former smoker, 40 pack-years, quit 10 years ago

patient.history_present_illness: A 67-year-old man with type 2 diabetes, COPD, and prostate cancer on active surveillance presented for evaluation of progressive bilateral ptosis, double vision, and difficulty chewing over 3 months. His wife first noticed his eyelids drooping approximately 3 months ago, initially intermittent and worse in the afternoons. He then developed horizontal diplopia when looking to the left, which was intermittent and positional. He began having difficulty chewing tough foods — he would tire out halfway through a meal and would need to rest his jaw. He has lost approximately 4 pounds over the past 2 months because he avoids foods that require prolonged chewing. He denies dysphagia with liquids but acknowledges occasional difficulty with large solid boluses. His voice has become softer and more nasal sounding after talking for more than 5 minutes, which his wife has noticed. He has no history of neck or back pain, no extremity weakness at rest, no falls, no bowel or bladder dysfunction. He was initially referred to ophthalmology who noted no structural eyelid pathology and no proptosis. He was then seen by his primary care physician who ordered brain MRI, which was reportedly normal. He was subsequently referred to the neurology clinic where examination revealed clear fatigability. His COPD is well-controlled on tiotropium with moderate exercise tolerance. The pulmonologist was concerned about overlapping respiratory muscle weakness potentially contributing to his reduced exercise capacity. He has not had any recent infections or antibiotic treatments. He denies weight loss beyond the 4 pounds from reduced food intake.

neurological_exam.additional: No active respiratory distress. SpO2 95% on room air.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Bilateral ptosis, left greater than right. MRD1 left 1.5 mm, right 3.0 mm. Fatigable ptosis on upgaze at 50 seconds. Limited abduction of left eye. Diplopia on left lateral gaze. No proptosis. Pupils 4mm symmetric reactive. No facial sensory loss. Mild bilateral facial weakness. Dysarthria noted after prolonged conversation.

neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented x4. Appropriate and cooperative. Normal language.
neurological_exam.motor: Shoulder abductors 4/5 bilaterally. Hip flexors 4/5 bilaterally. Neck flexors 4-/5. Distal strength 5/5. Fatigability demonstrated on sustained arm elevation.
neurological_exam.sensory: Intact to light touch, pinprick, vibration. No sensory deficit.

physical_exam.general: Weight 92 kg, height 175 cm. Well appearing.
physical_exam.respiratory: Prolonged expiration, scattered expiratory wheeze, no crackles. No accessory muscle use. Cough moderately strong.
